SmartHeal turns any smartphone or clinical device already in the clinician's hand into a clinical assessment tool. The assessment, measurements, photographs and evidence based record are done in seconds instead of 25 minutes, which puts clinical hours back into the day: more patients seen, more revenue earned per clinic, and more of each visit spent with the patient rather than on the write-up.

No extra hardware. No calibration stickers. No additional devices to buy or maintain.

SmartHeal walks the clinician through a best practice assessment step by step, taking the guesswork out, so the wound is assessed correctly the first time and in the same way by every clinician after that. The objective clinical record that compliance, accreditation and funding all rest on then follows the patient between roles of care, which holds the standard of care steady regardless of who is on shift and makes accreditation and reporting easier rather than harder.

Any wound, any metric, monitored from anywhere.

Australian owned, with Australian intellectual property and data hosted in Australia.

The problem

  • An amputation every two hours. Australia loses roughly 4,400 limbs a year to diabetes-related amputation, up to 85 per cent of them preventable with early detection.
  • Clinicians lose the day to driving and writing, not to treating. Podiatrists, wound consultants and community nurses spend much of the week on the road, then write the assessment up after hours at the end of a full caseload. A manual wound assessment takes 20 to 30 minutes. Done with AI it is a matter of minutes, with documentation completeness rising from 24 per cent to 70 per cent of required items.
  • Every trip avoided is a day of capacity back. In remote and rural delivery the dominant cost is moving the clinician, not treating the wound. When the person already on site can capture the wound accurately and a clinician elsewhere reads it, the trip becomes a decision rather than a default.
  • 450,000 Australians live with a chronic wound, at a cost to the health system of $3.5 billion a year, around 2 per cent of total health spend. One in four people with a diabetic foot ulcer dies within five years, and amputation rates are three times higher in remote Australia than in major cities.
  • Paper rulers and cotton buds are still the instrument. Every clinician records it differently, nothing lines up between visits, and nobody can tell whether the wound is healing.

Every wound needs four things. All four are failing today.

The solution

STEP 1
Photograph
One photo on the device already in the clinician's hand, at the bedside or in the community. Nothing to issue, print, attach or calibrate.
STEP 2
Measure in seconds
Length, width, area and perimeter returned automatically, with tissue estimation and a structured TIME assessment. The same wound, measured the same way every time.
STEP 3
Report before you leave
An audit-ready report generates on the spot. The visit ends with the documentation finished, instead of an evening of catch-up writing.
STEP 4
Track the trajectory
Every assessment builds one longitudinal record, so the next clinician sees whether the wound is healing rather than starting again from a fresh guess.
  • Hardware free. The established products need a bracket, a marker sticker or a dedicated device. We need none of them. There is no capital line for devices, which across a fleet of sites typically runs into tens of thousands of dollars, no consumables to re-order, nothing to ship to a remote site, nothing to lose and nothing to recalibrate.
  • Time back to the clinician. Faster assessment and more complete documentation at the same time, which is capacity returned to the caseload rather than paperwork moved around.
  • Capture locally, read remotely. A nurse or health worker captures at the bedside and a senior clinician reads and decides from anywhere. The expertise travels, the clinician does not.
  • The AI does the assessment work, not the clinician. Most tools on the market are a better place to record an assessment the clinician still has to perform by hand. SmartHeal produces the measurement and the structured assessment itself, and the clinician reviews, corrects and accepts it. That is the difference between digitising paperwork and removing it.
  • Consistency between clinicians and between visits. Every assessment is captured the same way, against the same structured framework, whether it is done by a senior wound consultant or by the newest member of the team. That means a handover reads the same to whoever picks it up, an escalation is triggered by a change in the wound rather than a change in who is looking at it, and the evidence behind funding and accreditation rests on one objective baseline instead of six opinions. It also makes a clinician's judgement easier to defend, because the record shows what was seen, when, and on what basis.
  • The patient can take part (patient portal, coming soon). A patient portal lets the patient or their carer capture the wound at home and share it with the treating clinician between visits, so deterioration is seen when it happens rather than at the next appointment. Published work on patient-facing wound photography reports higher engagement and a stronger sense of control over their own care.
  • Fewer trips, lower carbon. Sydney Local Health District has quantified what remote wound consultation supported by a wound AI app actually saves. Across 282 patients whose virtual consultation replaced a visit that would otherwise have been in person, more than 74,000 kilometres of travel was avoided, equivalent to about 13.4 tonnes of carbon emissions. Every visit that does not need to be made is emissions not spent, alongside the time and the cost saved.
  • Human in the loop by design. Explainable output, full clinician override, complete audit trail. Nothing enters the record without a clinician accepting it.
  • Data handling. Hosted in AWS ap-southeast-2 (Sydney), 100 per cent Australian data residency. Encrypted at rest with AES-256 and in transit over TLS 1.2 or higher, with tenant isolation between organisations and role-based access control.

Who we work with

Regulatory and governance position

  • TGA classification. Exempt Clinical Decision Support Software. It becomes ARTG Class IIa only if a regulated function is added.
  • Where the pathway goes. As SmartHeal increases the autonomy of the platform, that regulated threshold is one we intend to cross deliberately rather than accidentally: the next step is ARTG Class IIa under a full quality management system, with FDA clearance to follow for markets that require it. The current exempt position is a deliberate staging point, not a ceiling.
  • How the boundary is held. In the design decisions and in the product, by keeping human-in-the-loop as a compliance mechanism and not just a disclaimer. A clinician validates every output before it enters the record, and every output is explainable and traceable.
  • Quality management system. Aligned to the principles of ISO 13485, IEC 62304 and ISO 14971. Controlled draft, not yet certified.
  • Data. AWS ap-southeast-2 (Sydney), 100 per cent Australian data residency, AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2 or higher in transit, and tenant isolation between organisations.

Our story

SmartHeal was started by a clinician, not by a software company. Our founder spent seventeen years as a nurse and a doctor, and built this after watching the same wound treated three different ways by three different people, with the patient left to carry the consequences of that inconsistency.

Engineering is delivered by a senior team working to clinical direction.

Behind us sits an advisory board that is genuinely invested in SmartHeal and in what we are trying to do: people who lead clinical practice, innovation policy and health technology in this country and in the region, and who care about this mission as much as we do.
